title: cfDNA performance in low fetal fraction pregnancies
summary: Learn how Labcorp MaterniT® 21 PLUS addresses low fetal fraction with fetal enrichment technology, along with guideline recommendations and more
body_markdown:
In prenatal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening, also known as noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT), low fetal fraction can introduce uncertainty by increasing the potential for non-reportable results and the need for additional follow-up.


[MaterniT®](https://womenshealth.labcorp.com/providers/prenatal-screening/noninvasive-prenatal-screening) assay version 7 (AV7) builds on more than a decade of clinical experience and an extensive body of published evidence supporting cfDNA (NIPT) screening performance across diverse patient populations, including pregnancies with low fetal fraction. MaterniT AV7 incorporates a fetal enrichment step, which preferentially selects smaller cfDNA fragments more likely to be placental in origin. This enrichment reduces nonreportable results by approximately 30%, enabling more patients, especially those with higher maternal weight, to receive reportable results on the first draw. MaterniT AV7 represents the continued evolution of an already established screening approach, helping providers maintain confidence in challenging clinical scenarios.


## Understanding fetal fraction in prenatal cfDNA (NIPT) screening


Fetal fraction refers to the proportion of placental DNA circulating in maternal blood relative to the total amount of cfDNA in the sample. In prenatal cfDNA (NIPT) screening, sufficient fetal fraction is necessary to generate a reportable result.


Several factors may contribute to low fetal fraction, including early gestational age and higher maternal weight. When fetal fraction is too low, some screening assays may produce a no-call or nonreportable result, potentially leading to redraws, delayed information, additional administrative burden, and increased patient anxiety.


For providers, the goal is not simply to achieve a reportable result. Rather, it is to obtain clinically actionable screening information supported by documented performance and real-world experience.


## A clinical scenario: When low fetal fraction affects the patient journey


Consider a 34-year-old patient presenting for her first prenatal visit. Ultrasound confirms a gestational age of 9 weeks and 1 day, and she weighs 286 pounds. Following cfDNA (NIPT) screening, a nonreportable result due to low fetal fraction could trigger a cascade of follow-up steps, including redraws, ultrasound, specialist referral, genetic counseling to discuss the nonreportable result, and consideration of diagnostic testing, such as CVS or amniocentesis. This could equate to 2-6 weeks of unnecessary waiting and associated anxiety for the patient.


Situations like this are increasingly common in everyday obstetric practice. Providers need a screening strategy that can support confidence across a broad range of patients while minimizing workflow disruptions.


## Managing patient pregnancies with low fetal fraction in clinical practice


A low fetal fraction result does not necessarily indicate a fetal abnormality. As a screening test, prenatal cfDNA (NIPT) should be interpreted within the broader clinical context and in accordance with professional guidelines. The recent[Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) Consult Series #74](https://publications.smfm.org/publications/620-society-for-maternal-fetal-medicine-consult-series-74cell/) provides guidance regarding cfDNA (NIPT) screening and patient management, recommending cfDNA (NIPT) screening more broadly across all populations instead of only in high-risk pregnancies.1 In the setting of a nonreportable result due to low fetal fraction, SMFM emphasizes that follow-up should be individualized and informed by the patient's overall clinical picture, counseling discussions, and consideration of additional testing options for further evaluation if additional concerns emerge later in pregnancy. As with all prenatal screening decisions, appropriate follow-up should be based on individual clinical circumstances, patient preferences, and counseling discussions.


Aligned with the updated SMFM guidance, Labcorp's MaterniT platform uses an opt-in approach for additional screening features, including screening for sex chromosome abnormalities.


## Building confidence in low fetal fraction screening


Now that cfDNA (NIPT) screening is a routine option for all pregnant patients the ability to report results in low fetal fraction scenarios has taken on greater clinical importance.1 Earlier gestational age and higher maternal weight can contribute to lower fetal fraction and increase the likelihood of nonreportable results, making consistent screening performance a key consideration when selecting a cfDNA (NIPT) screening approach.

## Beyond performance: Supporting workflow efficiency


Many women's health practices manage growing patient volumes while navigating increasingly complex genetic testing decisions. Fragmented testing pathways can create administrative burdens and care coordination challenges.


MaterniT is part of Labcorp's broader testing and service offering that supports the entire pregnancy episode of care, including prenatal profiles, prenatal genetic and carrier screening, diagnostic testing, preeclampsia screening, and genetic counseling services. By working with a single laboratory partner, providers may benefit from streamlined ordering, reporting, counseling access, and continuity across the reproductive journey.


This integrated approach can be particularly valuable when additional testing or counseling is needed following a screening result.
